text: Here's the scenario: a new employee needs a laptop, a monitor, and a badge before their first day. HR submits an Equipment Request through the Service Catalog. Your job is to design the action sequence for the flow that automates this request, and decide which part is worth extracting into a custom reusable action.

Step one: Create Record. Triggered by the catalog submission, this action opens a formal Asset Request record on the asset-management side, populated from data pills off the triggering Request Item — employee name, start date, requested equipment, and the requester's manager.

Step two: Ask for Approval. Before IT provisions anything, the new hire's manager has to sign off. One named approver means this is approval from a specific individual. The flow genuinely pauses — a sysapproval_approver record is created, and nothing proceeds until the manager resolves it.
Step three: an If/Else branches on that outcome. Rejected means a Notify action tells HR and the requester why, and the flow stops there. Approved means the flow continues.

Step four: Update Record changes the Asset Request record's state to Approved, making it visible to the IT fulfillment queue. Notice this targets the record Step one created, not the flow's original trigger record.
Step five: a notification action fires an existing Notification to the IT fulfillment team's group, referencing the now-approved Asset Request so they know exactly what to prepare before day one.

Which step deserves to become a custom action? Step two — resolve the manager, run a single-approver approval. Every onboarding flow needs that exact pattern, so it becomes one reusable 'Get Manager Approval' action. Steps one, four, and five are specific enough to this request that they stay as ordinary actions inside this one flow.
A full flow, justified action by action. Next up: When to Build a Subflow Instead of a Flow, opening Chapter Four.
